title: Krishna pays his guru
hookLine: with Kamsa gone, Krishna goes to school, and the teacher's fee is a boy the ocean took
carry: the teacher is honored like a god
tomorrow: does Krishna remember the people who raised him?

lines: A FEE NO STUDENT COULD PAY.
cards: Kamsa is dead. His father Ugrasena is back on the throne of Mathura. Vasudeva and Devaki have their sons again.
So what does the hero of the story do next? He goes to school.
The Bhagavata's tenth book picks up the thread right after the arena, and sends Krishna and his brother Balarama to study with a teacher in the city of Avanti, a brahmin named Sandipani.
They sit at his feet like any other students. And when it's time to pay, the teacher asks for something no student could give.

teach.h: WHY WOULD THE LORD NEED A TEACHER?
teach.b: In the Bhagavata, Krishna is the Lord himself. Why would he need a teacher?
The text's answer, in paraphrase: the brothers, though they were the source of all knowledge, chose to live in a teacher's house to show the world how it's done. They serve Sandipani and learn fast.
Then comes the fee, the guru dakshina, the gift a student gives a teacher when the studies end.
Sandipani and his wife ask for the one thing they can't stop grieving: their son, lost in the ocean at Prabhasa. Not gold. Their boy.

At the shore, the ocean tells the brothers that a demon living in the shape of a conch, Panchajana, took the child. Krishna goes into the water, overcomes him, and takes the conch shell. The boy isn't there.

So Krishna goes all the way to the city of Yama, the lord of death, and blows that conch at the gate. Yama comes out, honors him, and gives the child back, and the brothers hand their teacher his son.

teach.h: THE TEACHER, HONORED LIKE A GOD.
teach.b: Hindus honor the guru, the teacher, like a god. An old Upanishad sends students home with that line: let your mother be a god to you, and your father, and your teacher.
It's why students touch a teacher's feet, why there's a day for teachers, Guru Purnima, and why the gift at the end isn't a fee that settles the account.

If the Lord himself sits at a teacher's feet, and goes to the gate of death to thank him, the rest of us can bow. That conch, Panchajanya, stays in the story: at the start of the Gita, it's the conch Krishna blows.

how: Hindus honor teachers by touching their feet and on Guru Purnima, and the custom of guru dakshina, a gift to a teacher at the end of study, continues in some traditional music, dance and scriptural schools; Krishna's fee to Sandipani is one story told when people speak of what a student owes a teacher.

a teacher's blessing given to a new student

s: Sandipani asked his well-known students for gold
he and his wife asked for their son, lost in the ocean at Prabhasa.
the conch Krishna took from Panchajana appears again in the Gita
Panchajanya is the conch Krishna blows on the battlefield at the start of the Gita.
the text says Krishna studied because he didn't know enough
it says the brothers, the source of all knowledge, lived in a teacher's house to show how it's done.

games.q: you're Krishna. your teacher asks for his drowned son back as your fee. what do you do?
o: go to the ocean, and then to the city of death if you have to.
explain kindly that the dead stay dead.
games.why: he goes to the ocean, overcomes Panchajana, then blows the conch at Yama's gate, and brings the boy home.

practice: Bring to mind one teacher who changed something for you: a schoolteacher, a grandparent, a coach, someone at work. Picture one thing they said, then ask quietly what you would give them, if you could, and let the answer come.
If you pray, hold that teacher in your prayer; if you don't, simply hold them in mind with thanks.

wordCard.voice: Guru dakshina. The gift a student gives a teacher when the studies end. Today, Krishna as a student, and a teacher's fee paid at the gate of death.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: guru dakshina, the gift a student gives a teacher when the studies end.

carryVoice: Your line: the teacher is honored like a god. Krishna paid his at the gate of death. Day nine hundred eighty-one, done.
